# Agents & Tool Use

*LLM first draft · unedited*

## The cost nobody could look up

The help desk from the earlier Modules retrieves before it answers now.
Someone types **my car will not start, and the depot is 27 miles away —
what will the tow cost?** The nearest handbook chunk comes back, and the
first half of the reply is right: in cold weather the engine may fail to
turn over, so hold the key down for ten seconds.

Then comes the second half. A 27 mile tow comes to about 88 pounds.

There is no 88 pounds. Today's tow rate is 4 pounds a mile, and it lives
in the depot price list — a page that changes on Mondays and was never
ingested. No chunk holds it, so retrieval could not have fetched it. The
model was handed a question, some fetched text, and one shot at a reply,
so it filled the gap with a plausible-looking number. It did the
multiplication in its head as well: `27 × 4` is `108`.

Two things were missing, and they are the same thing. The answer needed
work nobody had built into the pipeline — read today's rate, then
multiply — and the pipeline runs the same steps in the same order
whatever it is asked.

## A chain runs fixed steps; an agent picks the next one

That pipeline is a **chain**: steps you wrote down in an order, run top
to bottom, every time. Embed the question, fetch four chunks, paste them
into the prompt, ask. The model sits inside it as one step and decides
nothing about the shape of the run.

An **agent** is the other arrangement. The model is handed a goal and a
short list of things it is allowed to run, and each turn it picks one —
or decides it has enough and answers. Your code is the part that runs
whatever it picked.

The difference is one question: who decided the steps?

- in a chain, **you** did, when you wrote the code
- in an agent, **the model** does, one step at a time, while it runs

## A tool is a function with a name and a description

A **tool** is an ordinary function in your code that the model is
allowed to ask for. Nothing special about the function itself:
`rate_per_mile("tow")` reads a price list and returns `4.0`.

What makes it a tool is what the model is told about it. Three short
pieces travel with the question, for each one:

- the **name** — `rate_per_mile`
- the **description** — one line saying what it does: today's depot rate
  in pounds per mile for a named service
- the **arguments** — what it takes, and of what type: `service`, a
  string

That list is everything the model gets. It does not see the function
body. It never runs anything itself. It has no record of what the
function returned an hour ago. The description is the model's only
manual, so a vague one is a tool that gets picked at the wrong moment —
which is why that one line is where the effort goes.

## One question, worked one turn at a time

Three tools, and the question from the top of the page.

- `search_handbook(query)` — the handbook passage nearest a question
- `rate_per_mile(service)` — today's depot rate, in pounds per mile
- `multiply(a, b)` — two numbers multiplied

The model starts with the goal and nothing else. Read down the turns.

1. It picks `search_handbook("car will not start")`. Your code runs it:
   the question embeds to `[3, 1]`, the car chunk at `[2, 1]` comes out
   at about `0.99` against it where the banana bread chunk at `[0, 4]`
   is `0.32`, so the car chunk comes back — hold the key down for ten
   seconds.
2. That text goes back to the model under the goal, as the result of
   turn 1. Now it picks `rate_per_mile("tow")`. Your code runs it and
   hands back `4.0`.
3. Both results are in front of it. It picks `multiply(27, 4)`. Your
   code hands back `108`.
4. The goal and all three results go back one more time. This turn the
   model picks no tool. It writes the answer: hold the key down for ten
   seconds in cold weather, and a 27 mile tow comes to 108 pounds.

Four turns, three tool calls. None of that order was fixed when the code
was written. The model searched first because the question opened with a
fault, and it could not multiply before the rate came back.

Two details are what make the loop work at all.

- **Every turn re-sends everything.** The model remembers nothing
  between calls. Turn 3 works because the goal and the first two results
  are all in the message again, in full.
- **Your code runs the tools.** What comes back from the model is a name
  and some arguments — text. Whether that call is allowed, and what it
  does, stays yours to decide.

## The loop has a name: ReAct

Take the example away and four moves are left, going round:

1. the model reads the goal and everything that has happened so far
2. it picks a tool and its arguments, or decides it is done
3. your code runs that tool and takes the result
4. the result is added to the history, and it goes round again

The run ends when move 2 comes back with an answer instead of a call.

This is the **ReAct pattern** — reason about what is known, act by
calling one tool, then reason again on what came back. The name is worth
knowing because most agent libraries are this loop with comfort built
around it.

## Guardrails: a loop that can fail to stop

Move 2 is a model deciding it is done, and a model can fail to decide
that. The usual shape is dull: the same call with the same arguments,
turn after turn, each one paid for. Nothing inside the loop ends that —
the tool answers every time it is asked.

**Max steps** is the stop from outside: how many tool calls a run may
make before your code ends it. Against the four-turn run above:

- `max_steps = 2` — ends after `rate_per_mile`, before the multiply, so
  the run finishes with no answer. Saying that is the honest reply
- `max_steps = 5` — the run above finishes, with two spare
- `max_steps = 25` — a run that has gone wrong repeats its wrong call
  twenty-five times before anything stops it

Cost climbs faster than the step count, because of the re-sending above.
Five steps is up to six model calls, and each one carries more text than
the one before it.

Two more limits sit next to it.

- **A retry budget** — how many times one failing tool call is tried
  again before the run gives up. `2` is a normal number; a tool that
  failed twice is usually going to keep failing
- **What the model may not do** — the tool list is the whole surface it
  can reach, so a tool that deletes, pays, or emails is a decision
  rather than a convenience. The common rule: tools that read run on
  their own, tools that change something wait for a person

## When not to use an agent

If you already know the steps and the order they go in, write them down.
That is a chain, and it wins on all three of the things that matter:

- **Cost** — a chain makes one model call. The run above made four, each
  carrying more text than the last
- **Speed** — one round trip against four, one after another
- **Predictability** — a chain does the same thing today and next
  Tuesday. An agent's route is chosen while it runs, so the same
  question twice can take two different paths

Retrieval is the example. Every question wants the same three moves in
the same order — embed, fetch, ask — so there is nothing there for a
model to decide, and handing it the decision buys variability at four
times the price.

Reach for an agent when the next step genuinely depends on what the last
one returned, or when a question could need any of several tools and you
cannot tell which one in advance. That is the case the loop pays for.

## Three ways this goes wrong

From the outside these look alike — a wrong answer, or no answer.

- **Wrong tool** — the model picked a tool that cannot answer the
  question, usually because two descriptions overlap or one of them is
  vague.
- **Bad arguments** — the right tool, called with input it cannot use:
  `rate_per_mile("towing")` when the price list is keyed on `"tow"`.
- **Runaway loop** — the model never decides it is done, so one call
  repeats until max steps ends the run.

Telling them apart takes one habit: print each turn's tool name and
arguments beside the result that came back. Wrong name, and the
descriptions are what need work. Right name with arguments the tool
rejected, and the fix is in the argument description or in what the tool
says when it fails. The same call over and over, and it is the loop —
cap it, then look at whether any result ever told the model something it
did not already have.

## The loop, packaged

Libraries ship the loop so that you write the tools and not the
plumbing. In LangChain the `@tool` decorator turns a function into a
tool: the name comes from the function name, the description from its
docstring, the arguments from its type hints — which is one more reason
that docstring is worth writing carefully. `model.bind_tools([...])`
hands the list to the model, and an **agent executor** is an object that
runs the four moves round and round, taking `max_iterations` as its max
steps.

What the wrapper buys is that the loop stays the same whatever the tools
are. What it hides is every individual turn, which is exactly what you
want to see when an answer comes out wrong — hence the printing habit
above, and the second Module named below.

## What this leaves for later

Two Modules of their own, named here and needed by nothing on this page.

- **LangGraph** — the loop drawn out as nodes and edges with state you
  can see, for when one model deciding everything is too loose.
- **LangSmith** — every turn of a real run recorded and searchable,
  rather than printed and lost.

## The short version

- A chain runs steps you fixed in advance. An agent hands the model a
  goal and a list of tools, and the model picks the next step each turn.
- A tool is a plain function. All the model sees is its name, its
  one-line description and its arguments, so the description is the
  whole of what it chooses on.
- The loop is four moves repeated — read the goal and history, pick a
  tool or stop, run it, add the result. That is the ReAct pattern.
- Every turn re-sends the whole history, so cost climbs faster than the
  step count, and max steps is what ends a run that will not end itself.
- If you know the steps and their order, write a chain: cheaper, faster,
  the same every time. Keep the agent for when the next step depends on
  what came back.

# The grounded help desk from the Retrieval-Augmented Generation
# Module: fetch the nearest chunks, paste them in, answer from them.
# One message, one model call, no way to go and get anything else.
from langchain_chroma import Chroma
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI, OpenAIEmbeddings

store = Chroma(
    embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small"),
    persist_directory="handbook-store",
)
retriever = store.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 4})
model = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")

QUESTION = (
    "my car will not start, and the depot is 27 miles away. "
    "What will the tow cost?"
)

chunks = retriever.invoke(QUESTION)
context = "\n\n".join(chunk.page_content for chunk in chunks)

prompt = (
    "Answer using only the context below. If the context does not "
    "answer the question, say so.\n\n"
    f"Context:\n{context}\n\n"
    f"Question: {QUESTION}"
)
print(model.invoke(prompt).content)
# In cold weather the engine may fail to turn over, so hold the key
# down for ten seconds. A 27 mile tow comes to about 88 pounds.

# The first sentence is the handbook, word for word. The second is
# not: today's tow rate sits in the depot price list, which was never
# ingested, so no chunk holds it and no fetch could bring it back. The
# model had one shot at one message and filled the gap. The rate is 4
# pounds a mile today, and 27 x 4 is 108.
modelExamples.after:
# The same question and the same model, with two tools bound. The
# model now picks what to call and when to stop; your code runs
# whatever it picked and hands the result back.
from langchain.agents import AgentExecutor, create_tool_calling_agent
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI


@tool
def rate_per_mile(service: str) -> float:
    """Today's depot rate in pounds per mile for a named service."""
    return {"tow": 4.0, "jump start": 2.0}[service]

@tool
def multiply(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Multiply two numbers and return the product."""
    return a * b

tools = [rate_per_mile, multiply]
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "Use a tool for anything you do not already know."),
    ("human", "{input}"),
    ("placeholder", "{agent_scratchpad}"),
])
model = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
runner = AgentExecutor(
    agent=create_tool_calling_agent(model, tools, prompt),
    tools=tools,
    max_iterations=5,
)
print(runner.invoke({"input": "A tow, 27 miles. What will it cost?"}))
# rate_per_mile(service='tow') -> 4.0
# multiply(a=27, b=4.0) -> 108.0
# {'output': 'A 27 mile tow comes to 108 pounds.'}

# Two tool calls, both chosen by the model from the names and
# docstrings above, then it stopped and wrote the sentence. The 108 is
# arithmetic your code did, not a number the model produced.
modelExamples.caption: What moved: where the numbers in the answer come from. Before, one message reaches the model with the fetched handbook chunks inside it, so anything those chunks do not hold — today's tow rate, and the multiplication — is filled in, fluently and wrongly. After, the same model is handed two tools and picks them itself: your code reads the rate, your code multiplies, and both results travel back into the reply. The model still writes the sentence; it no longer supplies the facts inside it.

modelExamples.before:
# Routing by keyword: your code decides which function answers, from
# words it goes looking for in the question.
def search_handbook(query: str) -> str:
    """The handbook passage nearest a question."""
    ...


def rate_per_mile(service: str) -> float:
    """Today's depot rate in pounds per mile for a named service."""
    ...


def answer(question: str):
    text = question.lower()
    if "rate" in text or "cost" in text:
        return rate_per_mile("tow")
    if "handbook" in text or "manual" in text:
        return search_handbook(question)
    return "Sorry, I cannot help with that."


print(answer("what does a tow cost"))
# 4.0
print(answer("my car will not start"))
# Sorry, I cannot help with that.
print(answer("how much to be towed in"))
# Sorry, I cannot help with that.

# Every phrasing has to be listed somewhere. "my car will not start"
# holds none of these words, so the handbook chunk that answers it is
# never fetched, and "how much to be towed in" is a price question
# that says neither rate nor cost. A third tool means a third branch
# and a third word list to keep.
modelExamples.caption: What got hidden: the routing. Before, an if/else ladder decides which function runs, so every phrasing anyone might type has to appear in a word list — a question about a car that will not start matches none of them and falls through to an apology. After, each function carries a one-line description, the model reads the descriptions and picks, and both questions reach the tool that can answer them without sharing a word with it. The functions did not change; what chooses between them did, and a third tool is now a third function rather than a third branch.

selfCheckQuestions.prompt: A pipeline embeds the question, fetches four chunks, pastes them into the prompt and asks the model — the same four steps in the same order, whatever anyone types. Write down what that arrangement is called. Which comes closest to what you wrote?
selfCheckQuestions.explanation: Steps written down in an order and run top to bottom are a chain, whether or not a model is one of them. What makes an agent is the model picking the next step each turn from the tools it was handed, so the order is decided while the run happens rather than when the code was written. A model sitting inside a pipeline does not make that pipeline an agent.

A tool, because it is code the model can ask to run
